screens.title: Rates and dividends
screens.prose: Put-call parity with a dividend yield $q$ says $C - P = Se^{-qT} - Ke^{-rT}$. The blue line draws it for $S = \text{£}100$, $T = 1$. Move both sliders until it runs through the dots.
screens.question: Which slider turns the line, and which only lifts it?

options.text: $r$ turns it; $q$ lifts it without turning

options.why: $q$ sits in $Se^{-qT}$, which has no $K$ in it: it moves the line up and down. $r$ multiplies $K$, so it sets the slope.

options.text: Both turn it by the same amount
options.why: Only the term with $K$ in it can change the slope, and that is $Ke^{-rT}$.

hints.text: Which term of the formula multiplies $K$?
The slope is $-e^{-rT}$ and the intercept $Se^{-qT}$.
So $r$ sets the slope and $q$ the height.

feedback.correct: The slope is $-e^{-rT}$; the intercept at $K = 0$ is $Se^{-qT}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move one slider at a time and watch the line.

explain.text: Near $r = 5\%$ and $q = 1\%$ the line runs through the dots. The slope $-e^{-rT}$ depends only on $r$, and the height $Se^{-qT}$ only on $q$. So one line holds both inputs.

screens.title: The implied forward
screens.prose: Write $F = Se^{(r-q)T}$, the **forward**. Parity becomes $C - P = e^{-rT}(F - K)$, which is zero at $K = F$, as you found. Each strike then gives its own estimate, $F = K + e^{rT}(C - P)$.
screens.question: With $r = 5\%$, what forward does the 100 strike imply?

hints.text: Start from $C - P$ at this strike.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Grow $C - P$ by $e^{rT}$, then add the strike.

byKey.no-grow: You added $C - P$ as it stands. It is a value today; grow it by $e^{rT}$ to reach expiry.
byKey.discount: You multiplied by $e^{-rT}$. Going from today to expiry grows money, so multiply by $e^{rT}$.

explain.text: $C - P = 3.86$ today is worth $3.86 e^{0.05} = 4.06$ at expiry, so $F = \text{£}104.06$. Other strikes give slightly different values because of quote noise. We take the median over strikes, so one bad pair cannot move it.

screens.title: The dividend yield
screens.prose: The median forward for each expiry of the cleaned chain, from the strikes with both a call and a put. With $r$ known, $F = Se^{(r-q)T}$ gives $q = r - \ln(F/S)/T$.
screens.question: With $r = 5\%$, what dividend yield does the one-year forward imply?

hints.text: Take the log of $F/S$ first.

byKey.growth: That is $r - q$, the forward's growth rate. Subtract it from $r$ to get $q$.
byKey.sign: You added the growth rate to $r$. The forward grows at $r - q$, so $q = r - \ln(F/S)/T$.

explain.text: $\ln(F/S) = 0.0404$ is $r - q$ over one year, so $q = 0.0096$. The chain was built with $q = 1\%$, and the median recovers it to within 0.04 points.

screens.title: Fitting both
screens.prose: Why not fit $r$ and $q$ together, from the slope and intercept of a straight line through the dots? Here is that fit on the cleaned chain, at one month and at one year.
screens.question: Why is the one-month fit useless for $r$?

options.text: The tilt from $r$ is as small as the quote noise

options.why: The chain was built with $r = 5\%$ at every expiry. The fit failed; the rate did not change.
Four pairs would pin a line with a clear slope. The trouble is that the true slope barely differs from $-1$.
They are priced at $r = 5\%$ plus noise. The noise is what the slope cannot see past.

hints.text: Compare the true slope with $-1$ at each expiry.
At one month the true slope is -0.9958.
A slope that close to $-1$ moves $C - P$ by pennies across the strikes: the size of the noise.

feedback.correct: The slope carries almost no information about $r$ at short expiries.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at how far the true one-month slope is from $-1$.

explain.text: At one month, $r = 5\%$ tilts the line by only 0.0042 per pound of strike. Across the strikes that is a few pennies, the size of the noise, so the fit returned 0.84%. So we take $r$ from the rate market, a bill or overnight-index swap rate per expiry, and back out $q$.

screens.title: The spot is not the forward
screens.prose: A colleague centres every smile at the spot: he treats the 100 strike as at the money at every expiry. For a one-year option, $r = 5\%$ and $q = 1\%$.
screens.question: Where is the one-year forward, the true centre?

hints.text: The forward grows the spot at $r - q$.

feedback.correct: £104.08: the centre is £4.08 above the spot.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Grow the spot at $r - q$ for one year.

byKey.spot: You used the spot as the forward. Holding the share costs interest and earns dividends, so the forward is $Se^{(r-q)T}$.
byKey.no-q: You grew the spot at $r$ alone. The share pays a 1% dividend, which the forward does not get, so grow at $r - q$.

explain.text: The forward is $100e^{0.04} = \text{£}104.08$, so the centre moves by £4.08 at one year, almost a whole strike step. Measured from the spot, every strike's moneyness is off by about 4%: the 104 strike, at the money, looks 4% out of the money. One flat rate for every expiry is the same slip when the curve is not flat.

screens.title: From parity to the forward
screens.prose: You read the forward off the line and the dividend yield off the forward. Here is the same chain of steps for any expiry.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: $C - P = Se^{-qT} - Ke^{-rT}$, put-call parity with a dividend yield
$e^{rT}(C - P) = Se^{(r-q)T} - K$, multiply both sides by $e^{rT}$
$e^{rT}(C - P) = F - K$, name the forward $F = Se^{(r-q)T}$
$F = K + e^{rT}(C - P)$, add $K$ to both sides

hints.text: Start from parity.
Multiplying by $e^{rT}$ clears the discount on $K$.
Then name $F$, solve for it, and finally solve $F = Se^{(r-q)T}$ for $q$.

feedback.correct: Parity, grow to expiry, name $F$, solve, then take logs.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line must follow from the one above it.

byKey.s3: Naming $F$ needs $Se^{(r-q)T}$ on the right, which only appears after multiplying by $e^{rT}$.
byKey.s5: The log step needs $F$ first, so it comes last.

explain.text: Multiplying parity by $e^{rT}$ turns today's values into values at expiry. The forward then appears as $Se^{(r-q)T}$, and each strike gives $F = K + e^{rT}(C - P)$. Logs turn $F$ into $q$.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np
from math import log

# implied_forward is loaded, and clean = clean_quotes(make_chain()).

def implied_q(F, S, r, T):
    """Dividend yield from F = S exp((r - q) T)."""
    return r - log(F / S) / T

screens.title: A dividend announcement
screens.prose: The company announces a special dividend of £2.00, paid in six months. Shareholders get it; the holder of a one-year forward does not. Before the news, the one-year forward was £104.08 and $r = 5\%$.

state.caption: Parity line before and after the news

screens.question: By how much does the one-year forward fall?

hints.text: The forward is a price at expiry, in one year.
The £2.00 is paid at six months, leaving six months to earn interest.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Carry the £2.00 from its payment date to expiry.

byKey.flat: You took off £2.00 as if paid at expiry. Paid at six months, it would earn interest for the other six.
byKey.year: You grew it for a full year. It is paid at six months, so it earns interest for six.
byKey.disc: You discounted it. The forward is a price at expiry, so the dividend is grown to expiry.

explain.text: The forward falls by $2e^{0.025} = \text{£}2.05$, and the parity line drops by $e^{-rT}$ times that, £1.95. An American call holder may exercise just before the dividend to collect it. Lesson 6 prices that early exercise on a tree.

ideas: Parity with a dividend yield is a straight line in the strike: $C - P = Se^{-qT} - Ke^{-rT}$. It crosses zero at the forward.
Each strike gives $F = K + e^{rT}(C - P)$; take the median over strikes, and NaN under three pairs.
Short expiries carry almost no information about $r$, so take $r$ from the rate market and back out $q = r - \ln(F/S)/T$.

formula.name: Implied forward
formula.tex: F = K + e^{rT}(C - P), \qquad q = r - \dfrac{\ln(F/S)}{T}
formula.note: The forward, not the spot, is the centre of the smile.
